opus-5.5.text:
I think there are actually quite a lot of opportunities, more than people often assume. There's a common intuition that if you're not inside a frontier lab with access to the biggest models and the training infrastructure, you can't really do meaningful work on scheming. I think that's mostly wrong, though there are real constraints.

First, the constraints. External researchers don't have access to model weights for the frontier systems, they usually can't see the full chain of thought or internal activations, and they can't run interventions during training. So some research directions, like studying how scheming tendencies emerge over the course of training, or testing mitigations at scale during RL, are really hard to do from the outside. That's a genuine limitation, and I don't want to downplay it.

But there's still a huge amount you can do. A lot of our work at Apollo has been on evaluations: building environments where models have an opportunity and an incentive to behave deceptively, and checking whether they do. You can do that through API access. You can measure things like whether models sandbag on capability evaluations, whether they disable oversight mechanisms when given a goal that conflicts with the developer's, whether they lie about it afterward when questioned. Those findings have been taken seriously by the labs, and I think that's an important feedback loop.

Second, there's a lot of work on open-weight models. They're not at the frontier, but they're often good enough to show the precursors of these behaviors. You can do interpretability work, you can train model organisms of scheming deliberately and then study whether your detection methods catch them. Model organisms are a really useful paradigm because you know the ground truth: you put the deceptive behavior in, so you can check whether your probes or monitors find it.

Third, there's the science of evaluations itself, which is still very immature. How do we know an eval measures what we think it measures? How do we deal with models becoming increasingly aware they're being evaluated? Evaluation awareness is a big problem, because if a model behaves well specifically because it recognizes a test setting, your evals become much less informative. Working on that doesn't necessarily need frontier access.

And then there's monitoring and control: designing protocols that assume a model might be scheming and asking whether you can still use it safely. A lot of that can be done with smaller models standing in for untrusted ones.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that external organizations play a role labs can't play themselves: independent third-party verification. Even if the labs did excellent internal work, you'd still want someone outside who can credibly say "we checked this." So I'd encourage people to think of external research not as a second-best option but as a distinct and necessary part of the ecosystem. The main caveat is that it works best when there's a good relationship with the labs, so you get pre-deployment access and your findings actually influence decisions.

r001.rationale: The response says outside researchers can build evaluations using API access and check whether models behave deceptively.

r002.rationale: It mentions API access and smaller models, but does not say scheming evaluations require little compute.

r003.rationale: It discusses monitoring and control, but does not judge those areas to be underexplored relative to their promise.

r004.rationale: It proposes deliberately creating scheming model organisms with open-weight models, but does not specify using reinforcement learning.

r005.rationale: It says outside researchers lack frontier weights and cannot intervene during training, making work such as testing mitigations at scale during RL hard to do.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the opportunities are actually much better than people assume, and I say that as someone whose organisation sits outside the big labs.

Let me break it down a bit. There's a common intuition that scheming research requires frontier models and frontier compute, so if you're not at OpenAI or Anthropic or DeepMind, you're basically locked out. I think that's mostly wrong for a few reasons.

First, a lot of the most important work right now is conceptual and methodological rather than compute-bound. We still don't have a clean, agreed-upon definition of what scheming even is, or what a convincing demonstration would look like, or what evidence would make us update either way. Those are questions you can make progress on with a whiteboard and a few collaborators. And when we did the "Towards evaluations-based safety cases for AI scheming" work, that was fundamentally about structuring arguments, not about training anything.

Second, the API-accessible models are genuinely good enough to do meaningful empirical work. Our in-context scheming results — the ones showing models sometimes disable oversight mechanisms or try to exfiltrate what they think are their weights — those were done through standard API access. You don't need weights for that. The behaviours we care about show up in deployable systems, so you can study them in deployable systems.

Third, and this is maybe the part I feel most strongly about: the labs have a structural blind spot here. If you're inside a company, there are incentives — not necessarily bad faith, just incentives — that make it harder to publish an alarming result about your own model, or to design evals that your own model fails. External researchers can be adversarial in a way that's really valuable. The whole point of third-party evaluation is that the person checking isn't the person being checked.

Now, I want to be honest about the limits. There are things you genuinely can't do from outside. Interpretability work on frontier models mostly requires weights. Studying how scheming-relevant behaviours emerge during training requires training runs you can't afford. And there's a lag — by the time you've characterised something in the current generation, the next generation exists. So I wouldn't say external work is sufficient on its own. It's complementary.

What I'd actually encourage people to focus on is a few areas. Building better evaluations, especially ones that are robust to models recognising they're being tested — that's a huge open problem. Developing the science of what I'd call "evidence standards": when should a demonstration count, what's the right bar? Working on monitoring and control approaches that don't rely on the model being honest, because those transfer across labs. And doing the careful, slightly boring replication and red-teaming of claims that labs make about their own safety — somebody needs to be kicking the tyres.

The thing I'd caution against is spending a year building a very elaborate toy environment that doesn't connect to anything a lab would actually do. The most useful external work is the stuff that changes what the people with the models actually do on Monday morning. So I'd always ask: if this result came out, what would change?

r001.rationale: The response says API-accessible models allow meaningful empirical study of scheming and recommends external evaluation and red-teaming.

r002.rationale: It says important work is conceptual rather than compute-bound and that standard API access is enough for meaningful empirical work, making evaluation accessible outside the labs.

r003.rationale: The response recommends work on monitoring and control, but does not judge those areas to be underexplored relative to their promise.

r004.rationale: It does not propose using reinforcement learning to deliberately induce scheming in open-source models.

r005.rationale: It notes limits on outside researchers’ access to weights and training runs, but does not discuss limited fine-tuning of frontier models or its effect on anti-scheming training research.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot that researchers outside the companies can contribute. You can study whether models recognise when they’re being evaluated, whether they behave differently when they think they’re being monitored, and whether they can hide what they’re doing from an oversight system. Those are questions where external researchers can develop useful experiments and methods.

One distinction I’d make is between showing that a behaviour is possible and establishing how likely it is in a deployed system. If you give a model a goal and construct an environment where deceiving someone helps it achieve that goal, you might get a compelling demonstration of scheming. That’s useful, but you still have to ask how much your setup induced the behaviour and what the result tells you about more realistic settings. There’s a lot of valuable research in making those experiments more rigorous.

The main constraint is access. For some questions, an API is enough. For others, you want access to the weights, the training process, or internal checkpoints, and that’s much harder outside a company. So I wouldn’t expect external researchers to answer every question independently. But developing evaluations, testing oversight methods, and identifying failure modes are all areas where they can make substantial contributions. And having people outside the companies scrutinise the evidence is valuable in itself.

r001.rationale: The response says external researchers can test whether models recognize evaluations, act differently under monitoring, or hide behavior from oversight, and develop useful experiments and methods.

r002.rationale: It does not say scheming evaluations require little compute; it discusses API and model access instead.

r003.rationale: It does not judge AI control and monitoring to be underexplored relative to their promise.

r004.rationale: It does not propose inducing scheming in open-source models through reinforcement learning.

r005.rationale: It notes that access to weights and training is harder outside companies, but does not explain how limited fine-tuning of frontier models reduces the usefulness of anti-scheming training work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of room for people outside the companies to contribute. You can study many of the relevant questions using models that are already available: can you create a setting where a model has an incentive to deceive its overseer? Can you reliably tell when it’s doing that? And do the techniques you use to catch it still work when the model knows what you’re looking for?

One useful contribution is to make these questions much more concrete. Rather than asking, “Is this model scheming?” you build a particular test, explain what it measures, and investigate the alternative explanations for the behaviour you observe. That gives the companies something they can actually use and build on.

There are limitations, of course. An external researcher generally can’t study an unreleased frontier model during training, and access through an API can make some experiments difficult. So some work will require collaboration with a lab. But I wouldn’t conclude from that that you need to be inside a company to make progress. There’s substantial work to do on experimental methods, evaluations, and understanding which proposed safeguards actually provide evidence against scheming.

r001.rationale: The response says outside researchers can use available models to test whether they can induce deceptive behavior and reliably detect it.

r002.rationale: It does not say that scheming evaluations require little compute or are accessible for that reason.

r003.rationale: It discusses evaluations and safeguards but does not characterize AI control and monitoring as underexplored relative to their promise.

r004.rationale: It suggests testing incentives to deceive, but does not propose using reinforcement learning to induce scheming in open-source models.

r005.rationale: It notes limited access to unreleased frontier models and API constraints, but does not connect limited fine-tuning access to reduced usefulness of anti-scheming training research.
